opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot, because in the enterprise the economics really matter. It's not enough to be accurate; you have to be accurate at a cost that makes sense for the business.

The way I think about it is, first, you have to compare against what people do today. The traditional approach to predictive modeling over a relational database is incredibly expensive, just not in GPU hours. It's expensive in people. You have data scientists spending weeks or months writing SQL, joining tables, hand-engineering features, building pipelines, and then maintaining them. Every new prediction task, whether churn, fraud, or next-best-product, means repeating that process. So the hidden cost is enormous, and it's mostly human time and time to value.

When you move to learning directly on the relational data, treating the database as a graph where rows are nodes and primary-key/foreign-key relationships are edges, you shift that cost. You do more compute, but you eliminate most of the manual feature engineering. The model learns which signals across tables matter.

Now, on the compute side itself, there are a few things that make this tractable. One is that you don't need to process the whole database for every prediction. You sample a local subgraph around the entity you care about, say a customer, their transactions, the products they touched, and so on, a few hops out. That bounds the cost per prediction regardless of how large the database is. The second is that these models don't need to be gigantic. Unlike large language models, where you're paying for hundreds of billions of parameters to encode world knowledge, a relational model is reasoning over structured signals that are already in the data, so it can be much smaller and still very accurate.

And then with foundation models for relational data, the picture gets even better. Instead of training a new model for every task, you have a pretrained model that can make predictions through in-context learning, essentially zero-shot, and then you fine-tune only when you need that last bit of accuracy. So you amortize the expensive training across many tasks and many customers.

Finally, I'd contrast this with the approach of throwing an LLM at the tables, serializing rows into text and asking the model to predict. That tends to be both more expensive and less accurate, because you're spending tokens on formatting and the model isn't built to reason over millions of numerical records and their relationships. So I think the right architecture is a model that natively understands relational structure, and LLMs can sit on top as the interface, translating a business question into a prediction task.

So, short answer: compute is real, but it's bounded and getting cheaper, and compared to the human cost of the old way, it's a very favorable trade.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute on relational data but does not attribute greater GPU use to processing raw data instead of CPU-generated summaries.

r002.rationale: It says relational models can be much smaller than LLMs and contrasts them with the cost of hundreds of billions of parameters, linking model size to compute cost.

r003.rationale: It mentions repeated prediction tasks, but does not explain that frequent model-driven decisions make computational efficiency consequential.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually something I think about a lot, because when people hear "foundation model" or "pretrained model," they immediately think of something enormous that needs a cluster of GPUs just to answer a question. And that's really not the regime we're in when it comes to relational or enterprise data.

The way I'd frame it is that there are two very different costs: there's the cost of training, and there's the cost of inference. And then there's a third one that people tend to forget, which is the human cost of building the thing in the first place.

Let me start with that third one, because I think it's the biggest. Today, if you're an enterprise and you want to predict, say, which customers are going to churn, or which transactions are fraudulent, what actually happens is a data scientist spends weeks or months doing feature engineering. They're writing SQL, joining tables together, aggregating things over time windows, and then they train some gradient boosted tree on top of that. The compute for the model itself is trivial. All the cost is in the people and the time, and that process has to be repeated for every new task. That's really where the inefficiency is.

So from our perspective, the goal with these relational foundation models is to take the schema and the data as they are, the tables and the foreign keys, and let the model learn directly over that structure. You're essentially replacing months of manual pipeline building with something that can produce a prediction from a natural description of the task.

Now, in terms of the actual compute, the models we're talking about are much smaller than frontier language models. We're not operating in the hundreds of billions of parameters. The reason is that the data is structured. A row in a table is not a sequence of ambiguous tokens; it's a set of typed columns. And the relationships between tables are explicit. So the model doesn't have to learn the structure of the world from scratch; it's given a lot of it. That means you can get very strong performance from models that fit comfortably on a single GPU, and inference per entity is on the order of milliseconds.

The other thing I'd say is that the cost scales with how much of the database you actually need to touch for a given prediction. If you want to predict something about a customer, you don't need the whole database. You need that customer and their local neighborhood: their orders, their support tickets, the products they've looked at. So the way we set it up, you're effectively sampling a subgraph around the entity you care about, and the cost is proportional to the size of that neighborhood, not to the size of the enterprise.

And then there's the question of how often you have to do this. A lot of enterprise use cases are batch, you want to score all your customers once a day, and that's embarrassingly parallel and very cheap. The real-time cases, like fraud, where you need an answer in a few milliseconds, are the ones where you have to think more carefully about caching and about precomputing representations. But those are engineering problems we know how to solve.

So honestly, I'm not that worried about the compute. The thing I'd push back on is this assumption that moving to a learned approach means your cloud bill goes up tenfold. In practice, when you count the full picture, the compute is often less than what people are already paying to run all those feature pipelines in their data warehouse, and you've taken months out of the development cycle. That's the trade I'd make every time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses structured data and local database neighborhoods, but does not attribute greater GPU compute to processing raw enterprise data rather than CPU-generated summaries.

r002.rationale: It says these models are much smaller than frontier models, fit on a single GPU, and have millisecond inference, linking their smaller size to lower compute needs.

r003.rationale: It notes daily batch scoring and millisecond real-time decisions, then explains that real-time workloads require attention to caching and precomputation.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate the cost of learning from the cost of making a prediction. Training can be expensive, but you amortize that over many predictions. And in an enterprise database, a lot of the information is shared: customers buy the same products, transactions connect to the same accounts. You want to reuse that computation rather than process all of the data from scratch for every prediction.

The other question is, how fresh does the prediction need to be? If you’re predicting which customers might churn next month, you can compute those predictions in a batch. You don’t need to run the model every time somebody opens a dashboard. If you need a prediction in response to a transaction, then latency matters much more.

So I would think about it as a systems problem: what can you precompute, what can you share, and what actually needs to happen at prediction time? Those choices have a big impact on the cost.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reusing shared computation, but does not attribute GPU compute needs to processing raw data rather than CPU-generated summaries.

r002.rationale: It does not connect low inference cost to the models’ parameter counts.

r003.rationale: It mentions amortizing training across many predictions and says cost choices matter, but does not clearly state that frequent decisions driven by these models make computational efficiency consequential.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate the cost of training from the cost of making predictions. Training a model can be expensive, but you amortize that cost across many predictions. For a lot of enterprise use cases, you also don’t need to make a prediction every time somebody asks a question. You can compute predictions in a batch, write them back into the database, and then the application just looks them up.

The other consideration is how much of the data you actually need for a particular prediction. If you want to predict whether a customer will churn, you shouldn’t have to process the entire enterprise database for that customer. You want to pull together the relevant information and do computation on that. So the challenge is as much about organizing the data and the computation efficiently as it is about the size of the model.
